posts.text:
The U.S. Army sniper credited with 33 confirmed enemy kills survived six years serving in one of America's most elite military units. But after leaving the battlefield, Nicholas Irving faced a personal battle that nearly cost him his life.

His enemies knew him as “The Reaper,” while his fellow Rangers recognized him as one of the most effective snipers in their battalion. Yet the battle that nearly destroyed him began after he returned home.

Irving enlisted in the U.S. Army straight out of high school in 2004, determined to earn a place in the elite 75th Ranger Regiment. The journey was brutal. Years later, in an interview, he recalled that his selection class began with 85 candidates, but only seven graduated. He was one of them. Assigned to the 3rd Ranger Battalion, Irving progressed through demanding combat positions, serving as a machine gunner, assaulter, designated marksman, and sniper team leader. He also became the first African American sniper in his battalion.

During six years of military service, he deployed repeatedly to Iraq and Afghanistan, experiencing the realities of warfare that few civilians could fully understand. His defining deployment came in Afghanistan during the summer of 2009. According to his published military memoir, Irving was credited with 33 confirmed enemy kills during that deployment, a figure his publisher describes as a battalion record. His teammates and commanders gave him the nickname that would follow him throughout his life: “The Reaper.” His memoir also recounts a dangerous confrontation with an enemy sniper known as “The Chechnian,” one of the encounters that helped establish his reputation.

From the outside, Irving's military career appeared extraordinary. He had survived dangerous missions, earned the respect of fellow Rangers, and developed skills that made him one of the most recognizable American snipers of his generation. But surviving combat did not mean returning to civilian life would be easy.

When Irving left the Army, the structure that had defined his existence disappeared. There were no more missions to prepare for, no daily routines built around the men beside him, and no simple way to leave his wartime experiences behind. In a deeply personal interview with PBS, Irving revealed the seriousness of his struggles. He battled alcohol dependence and went through two rehabilitation programs. At one of his lowest moments, he recalled sitting with a bottle of whiskey and a pistol containing a single round. He felt like a burden. The man who had survived years of combat was now struggling to find a reason to keep living.

But that night became part of an unexpected turning point. Irving began writing notes on his computer. Those notes eventually developed into a journal, which became the foundation of his bestselling memoir, “The Reaper.” Writing helped him share experiences that had previously remained largely trapped in his memories.

However, Irving later explained that the greatest transformation in his life came from something entirely different. His son was born on November 28, the same date as Irving's birthday. He described his son's arrival as the moment he discovered a new purpose. After years of measuring success through military missions and objectives, he now had someone whose future depended on him. He wanted to provide his child with the kind of fatherhood he felt had been missing from his own upbringing.

His books went on to become bestsellers, he appeared on television, and he established HardShoot, a business focused on precision-shooting instruction. But perhaps his most meaningful achievement had nothing to do with a rifle.

For years, Nicholas Irving had been known by a nickname associated with taking lives. The turning point he described after leaving the Army came when he found a reason to dedicate himself to protecting, loving, and raising one.

The world knew him as “The Reaper.”

His son gave him another identity.

Dad.

That’s the first thing retired FBI whistleblower George Hill says when two FBI agents from the Philadelphia Field Office show up at his door on Ring camera — over a tweet.

The agents themselves indicate on the video they know it isn’t a real threat. They still came within 24 hours of Laura Loomer running to the top of the federal government. George is a 26-year military intelligence veteran and Marine (the FBI showed up on the Marine Corps birthday, no less), with five years at the NSA and 11 years at the FBI as a Supervisory Intelligence Analyst.

This is the “Good German” problem in real time. These agents, "Will" and "Brian," are just "ordinary men" who drove to knock on a door despite knowing it was wrong.  No principles to push back and say: “this is protected speech and not a threat.” Just compliance and "following orders." (They didn't even have the courage to leave a real business card with their names - just a blank one from the field office.)

The FBI showed who they were during the Biden admin. They knocked on doors over politics, protected speech, or thin pretexts. They sent a SWAT team over politics, religion, or your criticism of whatever admin approves their budget.
